# Caṅkī Sutta (MN 95 (PTS MN ii 164))

**ID:** MN 95 (PTS MN ii 164)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Caṅkī Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** With Caṅkī
**PTS:** MN ii 164
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Caṅkī Sutta* (MN 95; PTS MN ii 164) is an important discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya* addressing the epistemological status of Vedic revelation and the nature of spiritual education [Kalupahana 1976; Jayatilleke 1963]. Set in Kosala, the narrative opens with the renowned brahmin Caṅkī going to visit the Buddha despite objections from his fellow brahmins [Traces of Gandhāran Buddhism]. In the ensuing discussion, a precocious young brahmin student named Kāpaṭhika intervenes to affirm the undisputed validity of the ancient Vedic hymns [Jayatilleke 1963]. The Buddha criticizes reliance on unbroken oral tradition (*anussava*), comparing the succession of Vedic teachers to a line of blind men clinging to one another (*paramparāsaṁsattā*), wherein neither the first, middle, nor last can see [Jayatilleke 1963; Seeger 2005].

Central to the sutta is the Buddha's epistemological distinction among five grounds for accepting a view—faith (*saddhā*), personal preference (*ruci*), tradition (*anussava*), rational reflection (*ākāraparivitakka*), and cogitation upon a view (*diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti*)—all of which have a twofold result in this life, being capable of turning out either true or false [Kalupahana 1976; Jayatilleke 1963; Evans]. In response, the Buddha delineates a graduated path distinguishing the mere preservation or safeguarding of truth (*saccānurakkhaṇa*), awakening to truth (*saccānubodha*), and the ultimate attainment of truth (*saccānuppatti*) through personal transformation and meditative cultivation under a virtuous teacher [Evans].

Close parallels to specific pericopes appear in the Mūlasarvāstivāda *Vinayavastu* (*Saṅghabhedavastu*) and related texts [Peipina 2008]. Within the Pali canon, the sutta shares extensive formulas with other dialogues involving brahmins, especially the *Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta* (DN 4), *Kūṭadanta Sutta* (DN 5), *Ambaṭṭha Sutta* (DN 3), and *Tevijja Sutta* (DN 13), notably the standard list of ten ancient brahmin seers [Black 2011].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: SHT Sutta 25
- Passage-level parallels: AN 5.192 Doṇabrāhmaṇasutta; DN 13 (PTS DN i 235) Tevijja Sutta; DN 3 (PTS DN i 87) Ambaṭṭha Sutta; Kd 6 Bhesajjakkhandhaka
- Resembling parallels: SF 49; SF 67; SF 7; DN 4 (PTS DN i 111) Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta; DN 5 (PTS DN i 127) Kūṭadanta Sutta

**Sources**

- [Black 2011] Brian Black, 'Ambaṭṭha and Śvetaketu: Literary Connections Between the Upaniṣads and Early Buddhist Narratives' (JAAR, 2011) — Noted the shared list of ten brahmins in MN 95.13, DN 3, and DN 13.
- [Kalupahana 1976] David J. Kalupahana, Buddhist Philosophy: A Historical Analysis (1976) — Critique of divine revelation and the five sources of knowledge with twofold results.
- [Jayatilleke 1963] K.N. Jayatilleke, Early Buddhist Theory of Knowledge (1963) — Epistemological analysis of anussava, the student interlocutor, and the five grounds of conviction.
- [Evans] Stephen A. Evans, 'Doubting the Kālāma-Sutta: Epistemology, Ethics, and the 'Sacred'' — Distinction between saccānurakkhaṇa, saccānubodha, and saccānuppatti.
- [Seeger 2005] Martin Seeger, Phra Dhammapitaka und die Pali-Kanon-Debatte in Thailand (2005) — Citation of the blind men simile (paramparāsaṁsattā) at MN ii 170.
- [Peipina 2008] Lita Peipina, 'Pimgalātreya sūtra of the (Mūla)sarvāstivādins' (2008) — Textual parallels between Caṅkī Sutta, Cangī Sūtra, Pimgalātreya Sūtra, and Saṅghabhedavastu.
